[Experiments](index.html) · [Positive-shift construction](brasilfunc.html)

This notebook implements the $\kappa=0$ construction in
`Numerical_fractional_diffusion_IMAJNA_kappa0.tex`, particularly
`eq:gamma-scale`, `eq:rational-centered-scheme`, `eq:discrete-means`,
`thenumericalscheme`, and Section `sec:zero-shift-test`.
It follows the coefficient-table, partial-fraction, cached-factorization,
and load-vector logic of `brasilfunc.Rmd`. All functions are defined here;
this notebook neither sources nor rewrites that file or any existing
convergence notebook. The coefficient functions below are isolated copies
of its algorithms with a `kappa0_` prefix. The matrix routines use the
parallel names `my.fractional.operators.kappa0()` and `my.solver.kappa0()`.
They can coexist with the original functions in one R session.

Knitting defines the functions and executes small validation experiments.
`Matrix` is required; the rational branch additionally requires `rSPDE`
with its internal BRASIL tables. The spectral validation uses only
`Matrix` and base R. No MetricGraph, Rcpp, saved results, or continuous
spectrum is required by the numerical solver. The explicit tadpole
assembler below makes the independent check reproducible. For an existing
MetricGraph mesh, pass its consistent `mesh$C` and unshifted `mesh$G`
directly to the operator constructor instead.

```{r setup, purl=FALSE, dev="pdf"}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = TRUE, error = FALSE,
                      cache = FALSE, dev = "pdf")
if (!requireNamespace("Matrix", quietly = TRUE)) stop("Install Matrix first.")
```

## 1. Equation, FEM, and the constant mode

We solve
$$
 u_t+\nu A^\beta u=f,\qquad A=-\Delta_\Gamma,\quad
 \beta=\alpha/2\in(0,1],\quad \nu>0,\quad u(0)=u_0.
$$
The compact graph is connected, with continuity and Kirchhoff conditions
at every vertex (Neumann at a vertex of degree one). Thus
$A\mathbf1=0$. Constants are retained in the solution; imposing zero
mean on the entire problem would solve a different equation when the
data have nonzero mean.

As in `brasilfunc.Rmd`, assemble the consistent mass matrix $C$ and
stiffness matrix $G$. At zero shift $L=G$, and the coefficient matrix of
$A_h$ is $B=C^{-1}G$. It is self-adjoint in the $C$ inner product, not
necessarily symmetric in the Euclidean inner product. Fractional powers
are powers of $B$, not ordinary powers of $G$.

Put $c=C\mathbf1$ and $M=\mathbf1^Tc=|\Gamma|$. For coefficient vectors
and load vectors, respectively, the mean and centered part are
$$
 \bar U=\frac{c^TU}{M},\quad V=U-\bar U\mathbf1,
 \qquad \bar f=\frac{\mathbf1^TF}{M},\quad F_Q=F-\bar f c.
$$
Here $F_i=(f,\psi_i)$ is an **integrated load vector**, not nodal samples
of $f$. Initial conditions are projected by solving $CU^0=b_0$,
where $(b_0)_i=(u_0,\psi_i)$. In particular, $P_h$ preserves mass.
The coefficient projector $Q_hU=U-\mathbf1 c^TU/M$ and the load
projector $Q_h^TF=F-c\mathbf1^TF/M$ are different matrices.
Using `mean(U)` or subtracting the arithmetic mean of a load is incorrect.

For $t_k=k\tau$ and the time-averaged load
$F^{k+1}=\tau^{-1}\int_{t_k}^{t_{k+1}}F(t)\,dt$, backward Euler splits as
$$
 \bar U^{k+1}=\bar U^k+\tau\bar f^{k+1},\qquad
 (I+\tau\nu B_0^\beta)V^{k+1}
       =V^k+\tau C^{-1}F_Q^{k+1}.
$$
Consequently $\int_\Gamma U^n=\int_\Gamma U^0+
\tau\sum_{k=1}^n\mathbf1^TF^k$; zero-mean forcing conserves mass.
The constant eigenvalue must be exactly zero before its fractional power
is evaluated. Replacing it by a small positive shift introduces spurious
decay and is not the method in the paper.

## 2. Positive gap scale and the same BRASIL construction

There is no division by $\kappa^2$. Choose a fixed, mesh-independent
$0<\gamma_*\leq\mu_2$, where $\mu_2$ is the first positive eigenvalue
of $A$. The paper gives $\gamma_*=2/(|\Gamma|\operatorname{diam}\Gamma)$.
A certified upper bound $D\geq\operatorname{diam}\Gamma$ also gives the
safe choice $2/(|\Gamma|D)$. On the length-$(1,2)$ tadpole,
$|\Gamma|=3$, $\operatorname{diam}\Gamma=2$, so $\gamma_*=1/3$.
Conforming FEM has $\lambda_{2,h}\geq\mu_2$, hence the eigenvalues of
$Y_0=B_0/\gamma_*$ are at least one on the centered subspace.
A computed discrete gap alone is not a certified lower bound for all
meshes. The caller must provide a valid continuous gap bound when using
other graphs; the constructor cannot certify it from $C,G$ alone.

The BRASIL tables approximate $x^\beta$ on $[0,1]$. Exactly as in the
positive-shift notebook, their inverse-variable form is
$$
 S_m(y)=d_m+\sum_{j=1}^m\frac{\rho_j}{y-\eta_j},\qquad
 \eta_j<0,\quad\rho_j>0,\quad d_m\geq0.
$$
With $a=\tau\nu\gamma_*^\beta$, use
$$
 H_m(y)=\frac{S_m(y)}{S_m(y)+a}
       =r_\tau+\sum_{n=1}^m\frac{a_n}{y-z_n},\qquad
 r_\tau=\frac{d_m}{d_m+a},\quad
 a_n=\frac{a}{\sum_j\rho_j/(z_n-\eta_j)^2}>0.
$$
The $m$ negative roots $z_n$ of $S_m(z)+a=0$ interlace the
source poles. The copied helper brackets these real roots and checks the
partial-fraction reconstruction; it does not expand high-degree
polynomials. It reads an exact tabulated exponent when available and
otherwise linearly interpolates each source-coefficient column. Interpolation
preserves the checked signs but is not itself a new best-uniform
approximation certificate. The installed package determines available
orders and exponents, since these tables are internal `rSPDE` objects.

For $b=CV^k+\tau F_Q^{k+1}$ the sparse centered update is
$$
 V^{k+1}=r_\tau C^{-1}b+
       \sum_{n=1}^m a_n(G/\gamma_*-z_nC)^{-1}b,
 \qquad U^{k+1}=V^{k+1}+\bar U^{k+1}\mathbf1.
$$
This is the same shifted-solve formula as `brasilfunc.Rmd`, with
`scale.factor = gamma_star`, and with the mean handled exactly.
Each matrix is SPD because $G\succeq0$ and $-z_nC\succ0$; no inverse
of the singular stiffness matrix is formed. Factorizations are reused
for every step at fixed $h,\tau,\nu,\alpha,m,\gamma_*$. If any of these
changes, rebuild the operator. In exact arithmetic every solve preserves
$\mathbf1^TCV=0$. The implementation removes its residual mean after
combining the solves to prevent accumulated floating-point drift.
For $\alpha=2$ the method uses $(C+\tau\nu G)^{-1}$ exactly,
without tables or a rational approximation.

The full response to a load $v=CU^k+\tau F^{k+1}$ is particularly
convenient for the existing solver convention: compute
$q=\mathbf1^Tv/M$, apply the centered solves to $v-qc$, and return
$V^{k+1}+q\mathbf1$. Applying the rational transfer directly to the
constant mode instead would multiply it by $H_m(0)$ and lose mass.

## 3. Source coefficients and time-step partial fractions

The following is the parallel copy of the coefficient block in
`brasilfunc.Rmd`. Its `time_step * scaling` is now
$\tau\nu\gamma_*^\beta$.

```{r kappa0-coefficients}
kappa0_brasil_supported_orders <- function() {
    tables <- grep("^m_brasil[0-9]+t$", ls(asNamespace("rSPDE")), value = TRUE)
    sort(as.integer(sub("^m_brasil([0-9]+)t$", "\\1", tables)))
}

kappa0_brasil_coefficients <- function(m, beta) {
    stopifnot(length(m) == 1L, is.finite(m), m %in% kappa0_brasil_supported_orders(), length(beta) == 1L, is.finite(beta),
        beta > 0, beta < 1)
    table <- get(paste0("m_brasil", m, "t"), envir = asNamespace("rSPDE"))
    tolerance <- 32 * .Machine$double.eps * max(1, abs(beta))
    index <- which(abs(table$alpha - beta) <= tolerance)
    value <- function(column) {
        if (length(index) == 1L)
            table[[column]][index]
        else stats::approx(table$alpha, table[[column]], xout = beta)$y
    }
    poles <- vapply(paste0("p", seq_len(m)), value, numeric(1))
    residues <- vapply(paste0("r", seq_len(m)), value, numeric(1))
    constant <- value("k")
    if (any(!is.finite(c(poles, residues, constant))) || any(poles >= 0) || any(residues <= 0) || constant < 0 ||
        anyDuplicated(poles))
        stop("BRASIL table at m = ", m, ", beta = ", beta, " requires distinct negative poles, positive residues, and a nonnegative constant.")
    index <- order(poles)
    list(poles = unname(poles[index]), residues = unname(residues[index]), constant = unname(constant), m = as.integer(m),
        beta = beta)
}

kappa0_brasil_inverse <- function(y, coefficients) {
    stopifnot(all(is.finite(y)), all(y > 0))
    coefficients$constant + as.numeric((1/outer(y, coefficients$poles, "-")) %*% coefficients$residues)
}

kappa0_brasil_power <- function(x, coefficients) {
    stopifnot(all(is.finite(x)), all(x >= 0))
    coefficients$constant + as.numeric((x/(1 - outer(x, coefficients$poles))) %*% coefficients$residues)
}

kappa0_brasil_partial_fractions <- function(coefficients, time_step, scaling) {
    strength <- time_step * scaling
    stopifnot(length(strength) == 1L, is.finite(strength), strength > 0)
    p <- coefficients$poles
    r <- coefficients$residues
    constant <- coefficients$constant
    poles <- numeric(length(p))
    denominator <- function(y) constant + strength + sum(r/(y - p))
    for (i in seq_along(p)) {
        upper <- p[i]
        lower <- if (i == 1L)
            2 * upper
        else p[i - 1L]
        if (i == 1L)
            while (denominator(lower) <= 0) lower <- 2 * lower
        width <- upper - lower
        normalized <- function(t) {
            if (t == 0 && i > 1L)
                return(.Machine$double.xmax)
            if (t == 1)
                return(-.Machine$double.xmax)
            denominator(lower + width * t)
        }
        root <- stats::uniroot(normalized, c(0, 1), tol = 2 * .Machine$double.eps, maxiter = 1000L)$root
        poles[i] <- lower + width * root
    }
    residues <- vapply(poles, function(z) strength/sum(r/(z - p)^2), numeric(1))
    remainder <- constant/(constant + strength)
    stopifnot(all(is.finite(c(poles, residues, remainder))), all(poles < 0), all(residues > 0), remainder >= 0,
        remainder < 1)
    y <- 10^seq(0, 12, length.out = 257L)
    inverse <- kappa0_brasil_inverse(y, coefficients)
    expected <- inverse/(inverse + strength)
    actual <- remainder + as.numeric((1/outer(y, poles, "-")) %*% residues)
    reconstruction_error <- max(abs(actual - expected))
    if (reconstruction_error > 2e-12)
        stop("Inaccurate BRASIL time-step partial fractions: ", reconstruction_error)
    list(p = poles, r = residues, k = remainder, reconstruction_error = reconstruction_error)
}
```

## 4. Cached matrix operator and load-vector solver

`my.fractional.operators.kappa0()` has the same parameter order as
`my.fractional.operators.frac()`, except that its first argument is
explicitly called `G` and its scale is the positive gap bound.
`my.solver.kappa0(obj, v)` takes a complete load vector and returns a
numeric nodal coefficient vector. Both rational and integer branches
split the mean, so they share identical mass handling. Matrix inputs
must be a conforming consistent P1 pair on a connected Kirchhoff graph;
Dirichlet conditions, disconnected graphs, and mass-lumped inputs are
outside this notebook's assumptions. The constructor checks symmetry,
dimensions, positive mass, $G\mathbf1\simeq0$, and a successful mass
Cholesky factorization. These checks do not certify the full FEM model
or connectedness for arbitrary externally supplied matrices.

```{r kappa0-matrix-functions}
kappa0_positive_scalar <- function(x) {
    is.numeric(x) && length(x) == 1L && is.finite(x) && x > 0
}

my.fractional.operators.kappa0 <- function(G, beta, C, scale.factor,
                                         m = 1L, time_step, diffusion = 1) {
    stopifnot(kappa0_positive_scalar(beta), beta <= 1,
              kappa0_positive_scalar(scale.factor),
              kappa0_positive_scalar(time_step),
              kappa0_positive_scalar(diffusion))
    C <- methods::as(Matrix::Matrix(C, sparse = TRUE), "CsparseMatrix")
    G <- methods::as(Matrix::Matrix(G, sparse = TRUE), "CsparseMatrix")
    stopifnot(nrow(C) >= 2L, nrow(C) == ncol(C),
              identical(dim(C), dim(G)),
              all(is.finite(C@x)), all(is.finite(G@x)),
              Matrix::isSymmetric(C, tol = 1e-12),
              Matrix::isSymmetric(G, tol = 1e-12))
    one <- rep(1, nrow(C))
    c_one <- as.numeric(C %*% one)
    volume <- sum(c_one)
    stopifnot(is.finite(volume), volume > 0, all(c_one > 0))
    null_error <- max(abs(as.numeric(G %*% one)))
    if (null_error > 1e-11 * max(1, Matrix::norm(G, "I")))
        stop("G must annihilate the constant vector (Kirchhoff conditions).")
    factorize <- function(A)
        Matrix::Cholesky(Matrix::forceSymmetric(A), LDL = FALSE)
    obj <- list(C = C, G = G, L = G, beta = beta, m = m,
                scale.factor = scale.factor, time_step = time_step,
                diffusion = diffusion, one = one, c_one = c_one,
                volume = volume, null_error = null_error,
                mass_factor = factorize(C))
    if (beta == 1) {
        obj$LHS <- C + time_step * diffusion * G
        obj$factorization <- factorize(obj$LHS)
        return(obj)
    }
    if (!requireNamespace("rSPDE", quietly = TRUE))
        stop("The rational branch requires rSPDE with BRASIL tables.")
    coefficients <- kappa0_brasil_coefficients(m, beta)
    transfer <- kappa0_brasil_partial_fractions(
        coefficients, time_step, diffusion * scale.factor^beta)
    obj$coefficients <- coefficients
    obj$poles <- transfer$p
    obj$residues <- transfer$r
    obj$remainder <- transfer$k
    obj$reconstruction_error <- transfer$reconstruction_error
    obj$partial_fraction_terms <- lapply(obj$poles,
                                        function(p) G/scale.factor - p * C)
    obj$factorizations <- lapply(obj$partial_fraction_terms, factorize)
    obj
}

kappa0_check_vector <- function(v, n) {
    v <- as.numeric(v)
    if (length(v) != n || any(!is.finite(v)))
        stop("Expected a finite vector of length ", n, ".")
    v
}

kappa0_mean <- function(obj, u) {
    u <- kappa0_check_vector(u, length(obj$one))
    sum(obj$c_one * u)/obj$volume
}

kappa0_project <- function(obj, initial_load) {
    initial_load <- kappa0_check_vector(initial_load, length(obj$one))
    as.numeric(Matrix::solve(obj$mass_factor, initial_load, system = "A"))
}

my.solver.kappa0 <- function(obj, v) {
    v <- kappa0_check_vector(v, length(obj$one))
    next_mean <- sum(v)/obj$volume
    b <- v - next_mean * obj$c_one
    if (obj$beta == 1) {
        centered <- as.numeric(Matrix::solve(obj$factorization, b, system = "A"))
    } else {
        centered <- obj$remainder * as.numeric(
            Matrix::solve(obj$mass_factor, b, system = "A"))
        for (i in seq_along(obj$residues)) {
            centered <- centered + obj$residues[i] * as.numeric(
                Matrix::solve(obj$factorizations[[i]], b, system = "A"))
        }
    }
    centered <- centered - kappa0_mean(obj, centered)
    centered + next_mean * obj$one
}

kappa0_time_grid <- function(T_final, target_step) {
    stopifnot(kappa0_positive_scalar(T_final), kappa0_positive_scalar(target_step))
    N <- max(1, ceiling(T_final/target_step))
    list(N = N, time_step = T_final/N, times = seq(0, T_final, length.out = N + 1))
}

kappa0_evolution <- function(obj, initial, N, load_average,
                             keep_history = FALSE, max_history_mib = 256) {
    stopifnot(kappa0_positive_scalar(N), N == floor(N), is.function(load_average),
              is.logical(keep_history), length(keep_history) == 1L,
              !is.na(keep_history), kappa0_positive_scalar(max_history_mib))
    u <- kappa0_check_vector(initial, length(obj$one))
    times <- (0:N) * obj$time_step
    expected_mass <- sum(obj$c_one * u)
    mass <- mass_expected <- numeric(N + 1L)
    mass[1L] <- mass_expected[1L] <- expected_mass
    history <- NULL
    if (keep_history) {
        if (8 * length(u) * (N + 1)/1024^2 > max_history_mib)
            stop("Requested coefficient history exceeds max_history_mib.")
        history <- matrix(0, length(u), N + 1L)
        history[, 1L] <- u
    }
    for (k in seq_len(N)) {
        # Callback returns time-averaged integrated FEM loads, not nodal data.
        F <- kappa0_check_vector(load_average(times[k], times[k + 1L]), length(u))
        expected_mass <- expected_mass + obj$time_step * sum(F)
        rhs <- as.numeric(obj$C %*% u) + obj$time_step * F
        u <- my.solver.kappa0(obj, rhs)
        mass[k + 1L] <- sum(obj$c_one * u)
        mass_expected[k + 1L] <- expected_mass
        if (keep_history) history[, k + 1L] <- u
    }
    list(final = u, times = times, history = history,
         mass = mass, expected_mass = mass_expected,
         max_mass_error = max(abs(mass - mass_expected)))
}
```

For time-dependent forcing, supply the actual interval average in
`load_average(left, right)`. For example, if the load is
$F(t)=c+\sin(\omega t)b_\phi$, its average is
$c+\sin(\omega(t_k+t_{k+1})/2)\operatorname{sinc}(\omega\tau/2)b_\phi$
with $\operatorname{sinc}(x)=\sin(x)/x$ and $\operatorname{sinc}(0)=1$.
The time-grid helper adjusts $\tau=T/N$ to land exactly at $T$;
build the cached operator using this adjusted value.
The evolution driver stores mass diagnostics and the last vector by
default; coefficient history is optional and guarded. It advances every
step, unlike the autonomous spectral shortcut used below.

### 4.1. Detailed mapping of the paper's discrete means to the code {#discrete-means-code-map}

This subsection maps `eq:discrete-means`, `eq:rational-centered-scheme`,
and `thenumericalscheme` in the paper to the exact statements in the
functions above. Function names and quoted statements are used instead
of source line numbers, so the mapping remains valid when this notebook
is edited. The implementation retains a full coefficient vector $U^k$
between steps. It forms the centered vector inside the solver and restores
the mean before returning. In particular, **the forcing mean and centered
forcing are computed implicitly through a combined right-hand-side
projection**; there are no separate production variables named `f_bar`
or `F_Q`.

#### Objects and notation

In this subsection write
$$
 \mathbf e=\mathbf1,\qquad c=C\mathbf e,\qquad
 M_\Gamma=\mathbf e^TC\mathbf e.
$$
Here $M_\Gamma$ is the fixed graph length, whereas
$M_h^k=\mathbf e^TCU^k$ is the solution's time-dependent total mass.
They must not be confused. The P1 basis is a partition of unity,
$\sum_i\psi_i=1$, which gives
$$
 c_i=\int_\Gamma\psi_i(s)\,ds,\qquad
 M_\Gamma=\int_\Gamma1\,ds=|\Gamma|.
$$
The code uses the following objects.

| Code object | Mathematical object | Interpretation |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `obj$one` | $\mathbf e$ | Coefficients of the constant function one |
| `obj$c_one` | $c=C\mathbf e$ | Integrated load vector for the constant function one |
| `obj$volume` | $M_\Gamma=\mathbf e^TC\mathbf e$ | Graph length; independent of the solution |
| `u` in `kappa0_evolution()` | $U^k$ | Full nodal coefficient vector before a step |
| `F` in `kappa0_evolution()` | $F^{k+1}$ | Time-averaged integrated forcing load for the next step |
| `rhs`, passed as `v` | $CU^k+\tau F^{k+1}$ | Full right-hand side in load coordinates |
| `next_mean` | $\bar U^k+\tau\bar f^{k+1}=\bar U^{k+1}$ | Mean after the zero-shift step |
| `b` | $CV^k+\tau F_Q^{k+1}$ | Centered right-hand side in load coordinates |
| `centered` before the roundoff correction | Approximation to $V^{k+1}$ | Result of the centered sparse solves |
| The return value of `my.solver.kappa0()` | $U^{k+1}$ | Centered solution plus the updated constant component |

`U^k` is a vector of FEM coefficients, while `F`, `v`, and `b` are load
vectors. Multiplication by $C$ converts coefficients to loads; a mass
solve converts loads to coefficients. The two vector types have the same
length but require different formulas for their spatial means.

#### A. The shared denominator and the constant load vector

In `my.fractional.operators.kappa0()`:

```r
one <- rep(1, nrow(C))
c_one <- as.numeric(C %*% one)
volume <- sum(c_one)
```

These statements construct $\mathbf e$, $C\mathbf e$, and
$\mathbf e^TC\mathbf e$. The operator stores them as `obj$one`,
`obj$c_one`, and `obj$volume`, respectively. Since the mesh is fixed,
they are computed once and reused at every time step. `sum(c_one)`
means $\mathbf e^Tc$, so it is exactly the denominator in all three
expressions of `eq:discrete-means`.

#### B. The solution mean: the first formula in `eq:discrete-means`

The helper `kappa0_mean(obj, u)` returns

```r
sum(obj$c_one * u)/obj$volume
```

The multiplication `obj$c_one * u` is entrywise, and the sum is their
Euclidean inner product. Since $C$ is symmetric,
$$
 \frac{\sum_i c_i u_i}{M_\Gamma}
 =\frac{(C\mathbf e)^TU}{\mathbf e^TC\mathbf e}
 =\frac{\mathbf e^TCU}{\mathbf e^TC\mathbf e}
 =\bar U.
$$
This helper implements the paper's coefficient mean. Although it can be
called directly on $U^k$, the time-step solver obtains the updated mean
from the full right-hand side, as derived in D below. Its explicit call
to `kappa0_mean()` is used to remove the residual mean of the centered
numerical result after the solves.

#### C. The forcing mean and centered load: the second and third formulas

For a load vector $F$, the explicit equivalent statements would be

```r
f_bar <- sum(F)/obj$volume
F_Q <- F - f_bar * obj$c_one
```

These are explanatory statements; the production solver combines their
effect with the centering of $CU^k$. Indeed, by the partition of unity,
$$
 \mathbf e^TF=\sum_i(f,\psi_i)=(f,1)=\int_\Gamma f,
 \qquad
 \bar f=\frac{\mathbf e^TF}{M_\Gamma}.
$$
Thus `sum(F)` already represents the forcing integral. Multiplying `F`
by $C$ again would be incorrect: its entries are integrated FEM loads,
not nodal values of the function $f$.

Subtracting `f_bar * obj$c_one` gives precisely
$$
 F_Q=F-\bar f\,C\mathbf e,\qquad
 \mathbf e^TF_Q=\mathbf e^TF-\bar f M_\Gamma=0.
$$
For time-dependent forcing, `F` is the interval average returned by
`load_average(left, right)`. Therefore its mean is the interval-averaged
spatial mean, not an endpoint evaluation unless those coincide.

#### D. Why `next_mean` is the exact zero-shift mean update

In `kappa0_evolution()` the driver forms

```r
rhs <- as.numeric(obj$C %*% u) + obj$time_step * F
u <- my.solver.kappa0(obj, rhs)
```

Inside `my.solver.kappa0()`, the argument `v` is this `rhs`. Hence

```r
next_mean <- sum(v)/obj$volume
```

computes
$$
 \begin{aligned}
 \texttt{next\_mean}
 &=\frac{\mathbf e^T(CU^k+\tau F^{k+1})}{M_\Gamma}\\
 &=\underbrace{\frac{\mathbf e^TCU^k}{M_\Gamma}}_{\bar U^k}
   +\tau\underbrace{\frac{\mathbf e^TF^{k+1}}{M_\Gamma}}_{\bar f^{k+1}}\\
 &=\bar U^k+\tau\bar f^{k+1}=\bar U^{k+1}.
 \end{aligned}
$$
It is the **next** mean, not just the current solution mean and not
just the forcing mean. The recurrence has no denominator involving
$\nu$, $\gamma_*$, $m$, or $\tau\kappa^\alpha$, because here
$\kappa=0$ and the diffusion operator annihilates constants. The factor
$\nu$ multiplies diffusion only; it does not multiply the forcing term.

#### E. Why `b` contains exactly the paper's centered forcing

Immediately after computing `next_mean`, the solver executes

```r
b <- v - next_mean * obj$c_one
```

Substituting D and rearranging gives
$$
 \begin{aligned}
 b
 &=CU^k+\tau F^{k+1}
    -(\bar U^k+\tau\bar f^{k+1})C\mathbf e\\
 &=C\underbrace{(U^k-\bar U^k\mathbf e)}_{V^k}
   +\tau\underbrace{(F^{k+1}-\bar f^{k+1}C\mathbf e)}_{F_Q^{k+1}}\\
 &=CV^k+\tau F_Q^{k+1}.
 \end{aligned}
$$
This is exactly the load vector in `thenumericalscheme`. Consequently,
$$
 \mathbf e^Tb
 =\mathbf e^Tv-\texttt{next\_mean}\,M_\Gamma=0.
$$
The zero-sum condition applies to the load `b`. After a mass solve,
the coefficient vector $C^{-1}b$ satisfies
$\mathbf e^TC(C^{-1}b)=0$. It is not necessary that its coefficients
have zero arithmetic sum.

To make the equivalence explicit, the following expanded calculation
produces the same right-hand side in exact arithmetic:

```r
# Explanatory expansion of my.solver.kappa0(); not an additional time step.
u_bar <- kappa0_mean(obj, u)
f_bar <- sum(F)/obj$volume
V_current <- u - u_bar * obj$one
F_Q <- F - f_bar * obj$c_one
b_expanded <- as.numeric(obj$C %*% V_current) + obj$time_step * F_Q

v <- as.numeric(obj$C %*% u) + obj$time_step * F
next_mean <- sum(v)/obj$volume
b_combined <- v - next_mean * obj$c_one
# b_expanded and b_combined differ only by floating-point roundoff.
```

In projector notation, the distinction is
$$
 Q_{\mathrm{coeff}}=I-\frac{\mathbf e c^T}{M_\Gamma},\qquad
 Q_{\mathrm{load}}=I-\frac{c\mathbf e^T}{M_\Gamma}
                  =Q_{\mathrm{coeff}}^T,
 \qquad Q_{\mathrm{load}}C=CQ_{\mathrm{coeff}}.
$$
The solver's `b` is $Q_{\mathrm{load}}v$. The final identity explains why
centering the full load combines the two separate projections correctly.
The implementation never constructs either dense projector matrix.

#### F. Mapping the centered sparse solves to `thenumericalscheme`

The operator constructor stores

```r
obj$partial_fraction_terms <- lapply(obj$poles,
                                    function(p) G/scale.factor - p * C)
obj$factorizations <- lapply(obj$partial_fraction_terms, factorize)
```

Here `scale.factor` is $\gamma_*$, `obj$poles[i]` is $z_i$,
`obj$residues[i]` is $a_i$, and `obj$remainder` is $r_\tau$.
The stored `mass_factor` is the Cholesky factorization of $C$.
For $0<\beta<1$, the solver executes

```r
centered <- obj$remainder * as.numeric(
    Matrix::solve(obj$mass_factor, b, system = "A"))
for (i in seq_along(obj$residues)) {
    centered <- centered + obj$residues[i] * as.numeric(
        Matrix::solve(obj$factorizations[[i]], b, system = "A"))
}
```

The initial assignment is $r_\tau C^{-1}b$, and iteration `i` adds
$a_i(G/\gamma_*-z_iC)^{-1}b$. Together they implement
$$
 V^{k+1}=r_\tau C^{-1}b+
           \sum_{i=1}^m a_i(G/\gamma_*-z_iC)^{-1}b.
$$
`system = "A"` requests the solve with the original factored matrix;
it does not apply just a triangular factor. Neither $C^{-1}$ nor a
shifted inverse is formed explicitly. The input to these solves is
already centered, so the rational approximation never needs to represent
the true zero-eigenvalue response.

For $\beta=1$, the alternative statement

```r
centered <- as.numeric(Matrix::solve(obj$factorization, b, system = "A"))
```

uses the previously factorized $C+\tau\nu G$, giving the exact
integer-power centered backward Euler update. Its mean treatment is
identical to the fractional branch.

#### G. Mean preservation by each solve and the roundoff correction

For a shifted solve $(G/\gamma_*-z_iC)w_i=b$, multiply by
$\mathbf e^T$. Symmetry, $G\mathbf e=0$, and $\mathbf e^Tb=0$ give
$$
 -z_i\mathbf e^TCw_i=0.
$$
Since $z_i<0$, $\mathbf e^TCw_i=0$. Likewise, for the mass solve
$Cw_0=b$, $\mathbf e^TCw_0=\mathbf e^Tb=0$.
The integer-power solve satisfies the same property because
$\mathbf e^T(C+\tau\nu G)w=\mathbf e^TCw$.
Thus the assembled `centered` vector has zero FEM mean in exact arithmetic.

Finite-precision factorization, solves, and weighted summation can leave
a small residual mean. The solver removes it explicitly:

```r
centered <- centered - kappa0_mean(obj, centered)
```

R subtracts this scalar from every entry, so this is
$V\leftarrow V-\bar V\mathbf e=Q_{\mathrm{coeff}}V$.
It removes only a constant residual and leaves nodal differences unchanged.
The intended physical mean has already been saved as `next_mean`; it is
not discarded by this correction. This is also why the solver does not
center the full returned solution to zero.

#### H. Restoring the mean and deriving the discrete mass balance

The final expression of `my.solver.kappa0()` is

```r
centered + next_mean * obj$one
```

It reconstructs $U^{k+1}=V^{k+1}+\bar U^{k+1}\mathbf e$.
Therefore, in exact arithmetic,
$$
 \begin{aligned}
 M_h^{k+1}
 &=\mathbf e^TCU^{k+1}
  =M_\Gamma\bar U^{k+1}\\
 &=M_\Gamma\bar U^k+\tau M_\Gamma\bar f^{k+1}
  =M_h^k+\tau\mathbf e^TF^{k+1}.
 \end{aligned}
$$
For zero-mean forcing, $\mathbf e^TF^{k+1}=0$, so mass is conserved.
For nonzero-mean forcing, the mass changes by the supplied forcing integral;
it is not constrained to stay at its initial value. Floating-point
arithmetic introduces small discrepancies, which the diagnostics record.

#### I. Projection of the initial condition and mass diagnostics

`kappa0_project(obj, initial_load)` solves
$CU^0=b_0$, where $(b_0)_i=(u_0,\psi_i)$. Hence
$$
 \mathbf e^TCU^0=\mathbf e^Tb_0=\int_\Gamma u_0.
$$
This preserves the initial mass to the accuracy of the supplied load
integration and linear solve. The solver cannot correct an incorrectly
assembled initial load into the exact continuous projection.

The evolution driver independently accumulates the expected mass using

```r
expected_mass <- sum(obj$c_one * u)                 # initial mass
# Within each time step, after obtaining F:
expected_mass <- expected_mass + obj$time_step * sum(F)
```

and measures the returned solution's mass using

```r
mass[k + 1L] <- sum(obj$c_one * u)
```

The output `max_mass_error` is the maximum absolute difference between
the measured and accumulated expected masses over all recorded times.
Index 1 stores $t_0$, so R index `k + 1L` stores the mass after step $k$.
The expected value uses the actual supplied loads and therefore checks
discrete mass balance; accurate forcing quadrature must be checked
separately when comparing with a continuous mass formula.

#### J. The zero-forcing call in `true_frac_diff.R`

The animation has $f=0$, hence $F=F_Q=0$ and $\bar f=0$. Its time loop
calls the same solver with

```r
solution[nodes, step + 1L] <- .true_frac_solver$my.solver.kappa0(
    block$operator, block$operator$C %*% solution[nodes, step])
```

Here `v` is $CU^k$, so `next_mean` equals $\bar U^k$, and `b` equals
$C(U^k-\bar U^k\mathbf e)$. The solver diffuses the spatial variations
and restores the same mean. No forcing load needs to be assembled.
The installed MetricGraph logo created with `perform_merges = TRUE` is
connected: its run has one block, one constant mode, and one global mean.
The animation wrapper's component loop permits other graphs with several
connected components by applying this connected-graph solver separately
to each block. It does not disconnect or otherwise change the logo.


## 5. Independent tadpole assembly, loads, and quadrature

The tadpole has a stem of length 1 and a loop of length 2. Number the
free stem endpoint 1 and the junction 2, then the internal stem and loop
nodes, just as in the fallback tadpole construction in `brasilfunc.Rmd`.
Both loop endpoints map to node 2. On an interval of length $\ell$,
$$
 C_e=\frac\ell6\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 G_e=\frac1\ell\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$
Sparse assembly adds duplicate contributions, including both incidences
of a loop at its junction. Edge lengths are physical arc lengths;
there is no approximation of the loop length by polygon chords.
The supplied tadpole's diameter is exactly 2 and the scale is $1/3$.

Loads and errors use ten-point Gauss--Legendre quadrature on **each FEM
interval**. For the smooth sine benchmark this is more than sufficient
at the tested resolutions. Initial values are projected by a mass solve,
not interpolated at nodes. The quadrature nodes and weights below come
from the symmetric Jacobi matrix, avoiding an extra package dependency.
`kappa0_assemble_load()` accepts `function(edge, x)` with local arc
coordinate $x$, making it usable for other smooth data on this mesh.

```{r kappa0-tadpole-functions}
kappa0_gauss <- function(order = 10L) {
    stopifnot(kappa0_positive_scalar(order), order == floor(order), order >= 2)
    j <- seq_len(order - 1L)
    J <- matrix(0, order, order)
    J[cbind(j, j + 1L)] <- J[cbind(j + 1L, j)] <- j/sqrt(4*j^2 - 1)
    ee <- eigen(J, symmetric = TRUE)
    ii <- order(ee$values)
    list(x = ee$values[ii], w = 2 * ee$vectors[1L, ii]^2)
}

kappa0_tadpole_mesh <- function(h) {
    stopifnot(kappa0_positive_scalar(h))
    counts <- pmax(1L, as.integer(ceiling(c(1, 2)/h)))
    n <- 2L + sum(counts - 1L)
    inside_stem <- if (counts[1] > 1L) seq.int(3L, counts[1] + 1L) else integer()
    inside_loop <- if (counts[2] > 1L) seq.int(counts[1] + 2L, n) else integer()
    paths <- list(c(1L, inside_stem, 2L), c(2L, inside_loop, 2L))
    elements <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:2, function(e) {
        x <- seq(0, c(1, 2)[e], length.out = counts[e] + 1L)
        data.frame(edge = e, left = head(paths[[e]], -1L),
                   right = tail(paths[[e]], -1L), a = head(x, -1L), b = tail(x, -1L))
    }))
    ell <- elements$b - elements$a
    i <- c(elements$left, elements$left, elements$right, elements$right)
    j <- c(elements$left, elements$right, elements$left, elements$right)
    C <- Matrix::sparseMatrix(i = i, j = j, x = c(ell/3, ell/6, ell/6, ell/3), dims = c(n, n))
    G <- Matrix::sparseMatrix(i = i, j = j, x = c(1/ell, -1/ell, -1/ell, 1/ell), dims = c(n, n))
    list(C = C, G = G, elements = elements, paths = paths,
         h = max(ell), volume = 3, diameter = 2, gamma_star = 1/3)
}

kappa0_assemble_load <- function(mesh, fun, quadrature = kappa0_gauss()) {
    out <- numeric(nrow(mesh$C))
    for (j in seq_len(nrow(mesh$elements))) {
        e <- mesh$elements[j, ]
        s <- (quadrature$x + 1)/2
        x <- e$a + (e$b - e$a) * s
        values <- rep_len(fun(e$edge, x), length(x))
        stopifnot(all(is.finite(values)))
        w <- quadrature$w * (e$b - e$a)/2
        out[e$left] <- out[e$left] + sum(w * values * (1-s))
        out[e$right] <- out[e$right] + sum(w * values * s)
    }
    out
}

kappa0_phi <- function(edge, x) if (edge == 2L) sin(2*pi*x) else rep(0, length(x))

kappa0_tadpole_data <- function(h) {
    mesh <- kappa0_tadpole_mesh(h)
    c_one <- as.numeric(mesh$C %*% rep(1, nrow(mesh$C)))
    phi_load <- kappa0_assemble_load(mesh, kappa0_phi)
    # Enforce the analytically known zero integral at quadrature roundoff.
    phi_load <- phi_load - sum(phi_load)/mesh$volume * c_one
    initial_load <- spatial_load <- c_one + phi_load
    initial <- as.numeric(Matrix::solve(mesh$C, initial_load))
    list(mesh = mesh, C = mesh$C, G = mesh$G, initial = initial,
         initial_load = initial_load, spatial_load = spatial_load, phi_load = phi_load)
}

kappa0_l2_norm <- function(C, u) {
    sqrt(max(0, sum(u * as.numeric(C %*% u))))
}

kappa0_final_error <- function(mesh, u, exact, quadrature = kappa0_gauss()) {
    u <- kappa0_check_vector(u, nrow(mesh$C))
    squared <- 0
    for (j in seq_len(nrow(mesh$elements))) {
        e <- mesh$elements[j, ]
        s <- (quadrature$x + 1)/2
        x <- e$a + (e$b - e$a)*s
        uh <- (1-s)*u[e$left] + s*u[e$right]
        squared <- squared + sum(quadrature$w * (e$b-e$a)/2 *
                                 (exact(e$edge, x)-uh)^2)
    }
    sqrt(max(0, squared))
}
```

## 6. Exact discrete spectrum and autonomous reference

This is a **verification** routine, not the production sparse BRASIL
method. As in the isolated-$m$ reference in `brasilfunc.Rmd`, solve the
complete generalized FEM eigenproblem
$GV=CV\Lambda$, $V^TCV=I$ on a moderate mesh.
Writing $C=R^TR$, the symmetric matrix is $R^{-T}GR^{-1}$.
Here we first put the known normalized constant vector in the first
column of an orthogonal basis in these whitened coordinates, and
diagonalize its orthogonal complement. We explicitly set
$\lambda_{1,h}=0$ and $v_1=\mathbf1/\sqrt M$. This avoids raising
a roundoff perturbation of zero to a fractional power, and avoids
accidentally centering an arbitrary numerically perturbed eigenvector.
All remaining eigenvalues must be positive. Residual and mass
orthogonality checks detect an invalid decomposition. The dimension
guard runs before dense allocation.

For constant-in-time forcing, modal initial coefficients are
$a_0=V^TCU^0$ and modal forcing coefficients are $g=V^TF$.
With $d_j=\nu\lambda_{j,h}^\beta$, the exact semidiscrete and BE
solutions at $T=N\tau$ are, respectively,
$$
 a_j(T)=e^{-Td_j}a_{0,j}+\frac{1-e^{-Td_j}}{d_j}g_j,\qquad
 a_j^N=(1+\tau d_j)^{-N}a_{0,j}+
             \frac{1-(1+\tau d_j)^{-N}}{d_j}g_j.
$$
Both quotients equal $T$ when $d_j=0$. `log1p()` and `expm1()`
keep these formulas accurate near zero. The closed recurrence evaluates
exactly the same BE sequence for autonomous forcing; it permits the
paper's $\tau=10^{-6}$ check without half a million dense steps.
It cannot replace the time loop for general time-dependent loads.

```{r kappa0-spectral-functions}
kappa0_discrete_spectrum <- function(C, G, max_dimension = 1200L) {
    n <- nrow(C)
    stopifnot(kappa0_positive_scalar(max_dimension), n >= 2L,
              n <= max_dimension, n == ncol(C), identical(dim(C), dim(G)))
    # Twenty dense n-by-n arrays is a conservative peak-storage estimate.
    estimated_dense_mib <- 20 * 8 * as.double(n)^2/1024^2
    R <- chol(as.matrix(C))
    Rinv <- backsolve(R, diag(n))
    S <- crossprod(Rinv, as.matrix(G) %*% Rinv)
    c_one <- as.numeric(C %*% rep(1, n))
    volume <- sum(c_one)
    z <- as.numeric(R %*% rep(1, n))/sqrt(volume)
    W <- qr.Q(qr(matrix(z, ncol = 1L)), complete = TRUE)[, -1L, drop = FALSE]
    reduced <- crossprod(W, S %*% W)
    ee <- eigen((reduced + t(reduced))/2, symmetric = TRUE)
    ii <- order(ee$values)
    stopifnot(all(is.finite(ee$values)), all(ee$values > 0))
    values <- c(0, ee$values[ii])
    V <- cbind(rep(1/sqrt(volume), n),
               backsolve(R, W %*% ee$vectors[, ii, drop = FALSE]))
    GV <- as.matrix(G %*% V)
    CV <- as.matrix(C %*% V)
    residual <- GV - sweep(CV, 2L, values, `*`)
    denominator <- Matrix::norm(G, "I") * sqrt(colSums(V^2)) +
                   values * sqrt(colSums(CV^2))
    relative_residual <- max(sqrt(colSums(residual^2))/pmax(denominator, 1))
    orthogonality <- max(abs(crossprod(V, CV) - diag(n)))
    if (relative_residual > 1e-10 || orthogonality > 1e-10)
        stop("Zero-shift eigensystem failed residual/orthogonality checks.")
    list(values = values, vectors = V, diagnostics = data.frame(
        dimension = n, positive_gap = values[2L], relative_residual = relative_residual,
        C_orthogonality_error = orthogonality, estimated_dense_mib = estimated_dense_mib))
}

kappa0_autonomous_reference <- function(C, spectrum, initial, spatial_load,
                                        alpha, T_final, N = NULL, diffusion = 1) {
    stopifnot(kappa0_positive_scalar(alpha), alpha <= 2,
              kappa0_positive_scalar(T_final), kappa0_positive_scalar(diffusion))
    n <- nrow(C)
    initial <- kappa0_check_vector(initial, n)
    spatial_load <- kappa0_check_vector(spatial_load, n)
    V <- spectrum$vectors
    rates <- diffusion * spectrum$values^(alpha/2)
    a0 <- as.numeric(Matrix::crossprod(V, C %*% initial))
    forcing <- as.numeric(crossprod(V, spatial_load))
    if (is.null(N)) {
        log_decay <- -T_final * rates
    } else {
        stopifnot(kappa0_positive_scalar(N), N == floor(N))
        log_decay <- -N * log1p(T_final/N * rates)
    }
    gain <- rep(T_final, n)
    positive <- rates > 0
    gain[positive] <- -expm1(log_decay[positive])/rates[positive]
    as.numeric(V %*% (exp(log_decay) * a0 + gain * forcing))
}
```

## 7. Reproduce the paper's independent zero-shift check

Take $\alpha=1.2$, $T=1/2$, $\nu=1$, $u_0=1+\phi$ and
$f=1+\phi$, with $\phi=0$ on the stem and
$\phi(x)=\sin(2\pi x)$ on the loop. It is a normalized mean-zero
Kirchhoff eigenfunction with eigenvalue $(2\pi)^2$. Thus
$$
 u(s,t)=1+t+\left(e^{-at}+\frac{1-e^{-at}}a\right)\phi(s),
 \qquad a=\nu(2\pi)^\alpha,
 \qquad \int_\Gamma u(s,t)\,ds=3(1+t).
$$
The analytical eigenfunction is used for data and error evaluation only;
no continuous eigenpair enters either discrete solver.
The spatial table compares BE with this continuous exact solution at
$T$, at fixed $\tau=10^{-6}$. The temporal table fixes $h=1/32$
and compares BE with the **exact semidiscrete** solution, removing spatial
error. These are final-time $L_2(\Gamma)$ errors, rather than the
space-time norm used by the other convergence notebooks. They contain
no rational approximation, matching the paper's validation scope.
The expected rates are two in space and one in time; final digits and
roundoff mass differences may vary across numerical libraries.

```{r kappa0-paper-validation}
kappa0_paper_validation <- function() {
    alpha <- 1.2
    T_final <- 0.5
    rate <- (2*pi)^alpha
    exact <- function(edge, x)
        1 + T_final + (exp(-rate*T_final) - expm1(-rate*T_final)/rate) * kappa0_phi(edge, x)
    hs <- 1/c(8, 16, 32, 64)
    spatial <- do.call(rbind, lapply(hs, function(h) {
        data <- kappa0_tadpole_data(h)
        spectrum <- kappa0_discrete_spectrum(data$C, data$G)
        final <- kappa0_autonomous_reference(data$C, spectrum, data$initial,
                    data$spatial_load, alpha, T_final, N = 500000L)
        data.frame(h = h, error = kappa0_final_error(data$mesh, final, exact),
                   mass_error = abs(sum(data$C %*% final) - 3*(1+T_final)))
    }))
    spatial$rate <- c(NA_real_, log(head(spatial$error, -1)/tail(spatial$error, -1))/log(2))
    data <- kappa0_tadpole_data(1/32)
    spectrum <- kappa0_discrete_spectrum(data$C, data$G)
    semidiscrete <- kappa0_autonomous_reference(data$C, spectrum, data$initial,
                                               data$spatial_load, alpha, T_final)
    Ns <- c(5L, 10L, 20L, 40L, 80L, 160L)
    temporal <- do.call(rbind, lapply(Ns, function(N) {
        be <- kappa0_autonomous_reference(data$C, spectrum, data$initial,
                                           data$spatial_load, alpha, T_final, N)
        data.frame(tau = T_final/N, error = kappa0_l2_norm(data$C, be - semidiscrete))
    }))
    temporal$rate <- c(NA_real_, log(head(temporal$error, -1)/tail(temporal$error, -1))/log(2))
    stopifnot(max(spatial$mass_error) < 1e-10,
              all(spatial$rate[-1L] > 1.95), all(spatial$rate[-1L] < 2.05),
              tail(temporal$rate, 1L) > 0.98, tail(temporal$rate, 1L) < 1.05)
    list(spatial = spatial, temporal = temporal, spectrum = spectrum$diagnostics)
}

```

```{r kappa0-paper-results, purl=FALSE}
paper_check <- kappa0_paper_validation()
knitr::kable(paper_check$spatial, digits = 10,
             caption = "Spectral FEM: spatial errors and absolute mass differences")
knitr::kable(paper_check$temporal, digits = 10,
             caption = "Spectral FEM: isolated backward Euler time errors")
```

## 8. Sparse BRASIL validation at zero shift

The paper explicitly distinguishes its independent spectral check from
a dedicated zero-shift BRASIL study. This additional small experiment
exercises the new sparse implementation on the same nonzero-mean data.
At fixed $h=1/32$, $\tau=0.01$ and $T=0.5$, compare every rational
trajectory with exact-discrete BE on the same mesh, time grid, initial
projection, and load. Compute
$$
 E_m^2=\tau\sum_{k=1}^N (U_h^k-U_{h,m}^k)^TC(U_h^k-U_{h,m}^k).
$$
This isolates the rational contribution, like `conv_in_m_isolated.Rmd`.
The table also reports the final-time difference and maximum mass
balance error. Roundoff can limit improvement at high orders; a finite
sample is not a proof of the theoretical
$\exp(-2\pi\sqrt{\beta m})$ bound.

The checks compare a sparse step against the *same rational transfer*
evaluated on the discrete spectrum (testing scale, residues, and matrix
ordering), verify pure-constant forcing and zero-mean mass conservation,
exercise a genuinely time-dependent interval-average callback, and check
the exact integer-power branch against $(C+\tau\nu G)^{-1}$.

```{r kappa0-rational-validation}
kappa0_rational_validation <- function(orders = c(2L, 4L, 6L, 8L)) {
    data <- kappa0_tadpole_data(1/32)
    C <- data$C
    G <- data$G
    alpha <- 1.2
    tau <- 0.01
    N <- 50L
    spectrum <- kappa0_discrete_spectrum(C, G)
    V <- spectrum$vectors
    one <- rep(1, nrow(C))
    c_one <- as.numeric(C %*% one)
    reference <- vapply(seq_len(N), function(k)
        kappa0_autonomous_reference(C, spectrum, data$initial,
            data$spatial_load, alpha, k*tau, N = k), numeric(nrow(C)))
    table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(orders, function(m) {
        op <- my.fractional.operators.kappa0(G, alpha/2, C,
                        data$mesh$gamma_star, m, tau)
        out <- kappa0_evolution(op, data$initial, N,
                    function(left, right) data$spatial_load, keep_history = TRUE)
        difference <- out$history[, -1L, drop = FALSE] - reference
        error <- sqrt(tau * sum(difference * as.matrix(C %*% difference)))
        # Exact application of this rational transfer on the full FEM spectrum.
        transfer <- rep(1, nrow(C))
        S <- kappa0_brasil_inverse(spectrum$values[-1L]/op$scale.factor, op$coefficients)
        transfer[-1L] <- S/(S + tau * op$diffusion * op$scale.factor^op$beta)
        rhs <- as.numeric(C %*% data$initial) + tau * data$spatial_load
        modal_step <- as.numeric(V %*% (transfer * as.numeric(crossprod(V, rhs))))
        sparse_step <- my.solver.kappa0(op, rhs)
        transfer_error <- kappa0_l2_norm(C, modal_step - sparse_step)
        stopifnot(transfer_error < 1e-10, out$max_mass_error < 1e-10)
        data.frame(m = m, space_time_error = error,
                   final_error = kappa0_l2_norm(C, difference[, N]),
                   max_mass_error = out$max_mass_error,
                   sparse_vs_modal_error = transfer_error,
                   partial_fraction_error = op$reconstruction_error)
    }))
    op <- my.fractional.operators.kappa0(G, alpha/2, C, data$mesh$gamma_star,
                                        orders[1L], tau)
    constant <- kappa0_evolution(op, 2*one, N, function(left, right) c_one)
    conserved <- kappa0_evolution(op, data$initial, N, function(left, right) data$phi_load)
    omega <- 3
    average <- function(left, right) {
        z <- omega*(right-left)/2
        sinc <- if (z == 0) 1 else sin(z)/z
        c_one + sin(omega*(left+right)/2)*sinc*data$phi_load
    }
    forced <- kappa0_evolution(op, data$initial, N, average, keep_history = TRUE)
    # Independent modal time loop with precisely the same averaged forcing.
    a <- as.numeric(Matrix::crossprod(V, C %*% data$initial))
    S <- kappa0_brasil_inverse(spectrum$values[-1L]/op$scale.factor, op$coefficients)
    H <- c(1, S/(S + tau*op$diffusion*op$scale.factor^op$beta))
    for (k in seq_len(N))
        a <- H * (a + tau*as.numeric(crossprod(V, average((k-1)*tau, k*tau))))
    time_dependent_error <- kappa0_l2_norm(C, forced$final - as.numeric(V %*% a))
    integer_op <- my.fractional.operators.kappa0(G, 1, C, data$mesh$gamma_star,
                                               time_step = tau, diffusion = 0.7)
    rhs <- as.numeric(C %*% data$initial) + tau*data$spatial_load
    integer_error <- kappa0_l2_norm(C, my.solver.kappa0(integer_op, rhs) -
                      as.numeric(Matrix::solve(C + tau*0.7*G, rhs)))
    constant_error <- max(abs(constant$final - (2 + N*tau)*one))
    conservation_error <- max(abs(conserved$mass - conserved$mass[1L]))
    stopifnot(constant_error < 1e-10, conservation_error < 1e-10,
              time_dependent_error < 1e-10, forced$max_mass_error < 1e-10,
              integer_error < 1e-10)
    list(rational = table, checks = data.frame(constant_error = constant_error,
         conservation_error = conservation_error, time_dependent_error = time_dependent_error,
         time_dependent_mass_error = forced$max_mass_error, integer_error = integer_error))
}

```

knitr::kable(rational_check$rational, digits = 12,
             caption = "Isolated rational errors: zero shift, nonzero mean")
knitr::kable(rational_check$checks, digits = 12,
